📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How to buy and store fresh cranberries.

In a recent development, look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about.

Keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing.

Industry observers note that that vivid magenta filling is no food-coloring trick: Cranberries and plenty of lime give the curd its electric hue and tang. Let the pie set overnight, then pile on billowy meringue and break out the kitchen torch.

A 12-oz. bag of cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and about 10 minutes at the stove are all you need for this tangy Thanksgiving essential. Make it up to five days ahead and save any leftovers for turkey-cranberry sliders.

Sources indicate that layers of tender buttermilk cake, tart cranberry jam, and silky white chocolate frosting make an excellent argument for serving cake on Thanksgiving. The sugared cranberries on top are like little sour candies.

Industry observers note that imagine Key lime pie dressed for the holidays. The punchy cranberry-lime curd meets a crisp press-in crust made with gingersnaps and pecans. A generous dollop of whipped cream rounds out the tartness.

Sources indicate that here’s a reason to keep canned cranberry sauce around after Thanksgiving. Jellied sauce melts into a glossy, sweet-and-sour glaze that coats chicken and green beans. Think orange chicken, with a cranberry twist.

Cranberries turn this classic upside-down apple tart a beautiful rosy pink while cutting through its buttery sweetness. Homemade rough puff pastry supplies the flaky base; vanilla ice cream is very much encouraged.

Canned whole-berry cranberry sauce becomes a punchy dressing for pleasantly bitter endive and frisée. Add crunchy candied pecans and salty Manchego, and suddenly cranberry sauce is doing salad duty.

Two layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust surround a tart cranberry filling in this striking take on a Linzer torte. Save it for a holiday dessert table—or any occasion that calls for something special.

Dress crisp-bottomed Persian rice with dried cranberries, saffron, and fragrant herbs. The berries plump in ghee alongside rosemary, sage, and thyme, adding little pops of sweetness against the savory rice.

Recent findings suggest that if the wobble is the best part of canned cranberry sauce for you, this homemade version delivers. It’s sliceable, deeply fruity, and subtly fragrant with cardamom and bay leaves. Bring on the ridges.

It has been revealed that roasted brussels sprouts get a lively companion in cranberry mostarda, a sweet-tart condiment with mustard seeds, prunes, and a little brandy. Make extra mostarda: It belongs on more than just sprouts.

In a recent development, A warm cranberry-apple topping brings plenty of tart fruit flavor to this crowd-friendly baked oatmeal. It’s a welcome breakfast when the house is full and everyone seems to wake up hungry at once.

Rum, hard cider, cranberry juice, ginger ale, and lime make a lively batch cocktail. Cranberry-studded ice cubes do double duty, keeping glasses cold and making the punch look party-ready.

Recent findings suggest that jalapeño and lime give classic cranberry sauce a bright, spicy kick. It’s especially good alongside roasted meats or piled onto a leftover turkey sandwich when you want something with a little heat.

Forget the giant roast bird for a minute. These tender, gravy-coated turkey meatballs come with a cranberry-orange marmalade jam that stands in for traditional lingonberries. A heap of mashed potatoes completes the picture.

Fresh ginger gives this cranberry relish some zip, while golden raisins and allspice round out its tartness. Spoon it onto a cheese board or save the leftovers for French toast the next morning.

Herbs in the dredge give this crunchy fried chicken Thanksgiving energy, but the quick cranberry-mustard dipping sauce is the real holiday flourish. It’s a compelling alternative to roasting an entire turkey.

Sources indicate that homemade cranberry-thyme syrup, Campari, and Champagne make a sparkling cocktail that’s fruity, pleasantly bitter, and dressed for a party. Make the syrup up to two weeks ahead; the drinks come together in minutes.

Sources indicate that boxed stuffing mix gets a serious upgrade with aromatic vegetables, dried cranberries, and the savory drippings from crisp-skinned chicken thighs. It’s Thanksgiving-adjacent comfort food, made in one skillet any night of the week.

Industry observers note that roasted sweet potatoes and delicata squash get a glossy, sweet-and-sour cranberry sauce made with red wine vinegar and thyme. Make extra: The agrodolce is just as good spooned over Thanksgiving turkey.

Whole orange and a cinnamon stick give this chunky cranberry sauce its fragrant warmth. Blanching the chopped orange first keeps bitterness in check, while a little butter softens the berries’ sharp edge.

Industry observers note that A buttery, lemony custard studded with tart cranberries gives this Southern classic a holiday spin. The berries stay mostly intact, offering juicy little bursts of tartness against the rich filling.

Dried figs bring earthy sweetness to this bold cranberry chutney, while ginger, vinegar, and whole grain mustard keep it lively. It’s the sort of condiment you’ll want beside roast pork as much as turkey.

Dorie Greenspan’s warmly spiced Bundt packs in fresh and dried cranberries, toasted almonds, and a little five-spice powder. Greek yogurt keeps the cake rich; orange icing supplies the finishing flourish.

Industry observers note that baker Amanda Mack tucks a tart cranberry-orange filling into exceptionally flaky buttermilk pastry for individual pies. They’re a thoughtful addition to a dessert spread where everyone wants to try a little of everything.

No simmering required for this bright, crunchy cranberry relish. Walnuts, shallot, mustard seeds, and Fresno chile give it plenty of texture and bite—a particularly good counterpoint to rich holiday mains.

Homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail its fruity punch. Lime juice keeps it lively, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim makes each glass taste decidedly more festive than a typical margarita.

Chopped fresh cranberries bring little bursts of tartness to an otherwise classic cheddar grilled cheese. A swipe of Dijon mustard ties the flavors together. Sometimes the best cranberry recipe is also lunch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

According to recent reports, now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner Upcoming Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.).

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the Latest England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”.

Earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at Newly introduced Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance released in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

Recent findings suggest that while conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

Recent findings suggest that “I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani indicates. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a big change. They understand what I want.”.

Recent findings suggest that ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, Upcoming Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”.

Sources indicate that while some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”.

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” notes Masahiro Uchida, Upcoming Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”.

Sources indicate that at 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his New Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

Recent findings suggest that ohtani still intends on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”.

What words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”.

Tech Report: Thanksgiving Cornbread

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing).
  • Recent findings suggest that the intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

Recent findings suggest that the intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

In a recent development, cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Recent findings suggest that stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

In a recent development, bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

Sources indicate that these eight recipes made hosting our first Friendsgiving in our small Latest York City apartment a breeze. I will be honest, we did have a little mishap. Industry observers note that if you want the easiest Friendsgiving with the tastiest recipes, these are eight I would recommend. All of my friends loved them, and they made for a night of amazing memories. I hope you enjoy them just as much as we did!

According to recent reports, we engineered this bite-sized app to have everything you could ever want in a holiday appetizer, all in one bite: a flaky pastry base made from crescent dough, sweet cranberry sauce, rich, cheesy brie, and crunchy pecans. Ready in a little over 30 minutes, these bites are the ideal last-minute appetizer, and are so good, they just might steal the show at your Thanksgiving dinner.

Slow-cooked turkey legs are this year’s ultimate Thanksgiving hack. No basting, no inevitable dry meat—no fuss at all. All you have to do is make an easy festive herb butter, wrap everything in foil, and let it roast unsupervised. This recipe allows for all of the Thanksgiving sides that really can’t fit in your oven alongside a 15-pound turkey.

It has been revealed that think glazed sweet potatoes always need brown sugar, orange juice, or pecans? Think again. Coated in a savory maple-miso sauce, these melting sweet potatoes are here to challenge everything you think a sweet potato can be—and win you over with their deliciousness.

Croissant stuffing brings the light, airy texture of French pastry straight to your Thanksgiving table. While most traditional stuffings rely on denser breads, I opted for croissants to create a lighter, fluffier bite, and the result is everything. Trust me, this is the stuffing that has everything—savory, sweet, a little crunch, a bit of freshness—all tossed together with dreamy croissants in your 13" x 9" pan.

The perfect mac & cheese will have you dreaming about its cheesy goodness for days after you eat it. Obviously, the cheese has to be top-notch, but the real secret to the best version is the perfect crunchy topping. My recipe delivers on all of that and more, so you won't even think about reaching for another mac & cheese recipe for the rest of your gatherings.

In a recent development, while I love a hot toddy or spiked apple cider, mulled wine is the warming, boozy beverage I love to cozy up to as soon as the weather starts to grow cold. My classic recipe uses red wine, traditional warming spices, and brandy to create the perfect holiday drink to serve a crowd—or just yourself, no judgment here!

Recent findings suggest that this fall-flavored iced tea is made with brewed black tea, apple cider, and maple syrup for a cooling drink to welcome the transition between summer and fall. Serve it for game day to wash down seven-layer dip and pigs in a blanket, or sip it as an afternoon pick-me-up that’s just sweet enough and totally refreshing.

Industry observers note that are you tired of spending hours making apple pie but still obsessed with the flavors of this beloved fall dessert? I have the perfect solution—crescent apple dumplings. The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

According to recent reports, the chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans quickly filled the comments with condolences and support.

“Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

Recent findings suggest that others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve concerns or celebrate the wins,” he said in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he said, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”.

And judging by the outpouring of love from fans, friends, and loved ones in the comments, the Fieri’s can take comfort knowing Jim left a lasting impression on more people than just his family.

#134662. Latest Update: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

📅 11 Nov 2020 • ⏱️ 33m • 📚 Deep Dive (6680 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

📅 11 Nov 2020 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop.
  • New in this update: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options.
  • A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop. But the best cutting boards do more than just protect your counters during food prep—they provide a stable surface when you’re vigorously chopping and act as a protective surface that prevents prematurely dulling the blades of your kitchen knives. Cutting boards come in a variety of materials: plastic, wood, rubber, even glass and metal for inexplicable reasons. After testing dozens of boards of all sorts of materials over the course of six years, we have found five favorites. Read on to find out which might be best for you as well as how we tested and what we look for in the cutting boards we want to use every day.

New in this update: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options. They’re easier on knives and more beautiful to keep on the counter. And our new top pick is reasonably priced as end-grain boards go. For more on what makes end- and edge-grain boards different, click here. And if you’re looking for a quality (but truly inexpensive) wood board, we’d encourage you to look at these two Boos boards. They’re edge-grain, so they’ll wear your knives more quickly, but Boos makes almost universally great cutting boards.

Maple End-Grain Cutting Board (18" x 12").

A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment. A good wood cutting board can last decades and decades, and since it will likely live permanently on your counter, function as a key aesthetic component of your kitchen. Our editors have used this heavy-duty piece for over a year in their home kitchens, and even after daily use, it indicates little to no wear and only minimal staining.

What we love: The craftsmanship on the board is apparent as soon as you take it out of the box. The offset pattern of the individual pieces of wood is striking (as it is on most end-grain boards). And its construction feels smooth and solid.

As an end-grain board, it’s easy on knife blades, leaving them sharper than a less expensive edge-grain board. The real highlights, beyond the pure aesthetics, are in the small design features, though. Senior shopping editor Noah Kaufman has been using it in his home kitchen since June of 2025 and has found it the most stable board he’s ever used. That’s thanks to the addition of four grippy silicone-tipped feet on one side (you can order a Boardsmith without the feet, but you’d be giving away that stability). Those feet also raise the board up a little higher on the counter—which prevents the underside from retaining moisture and warping—and for Noah, they elevate the board to a very comfortable cutting height. It’s also reversible, with an effective, though not too deep, juice groove on the side of the footed side.

Boardsmith’s end-grain boards are very customizable. They come in four sizes (we tested the 18" x 12" x 2", but the largest—24" x 18" x 2"—would make a beautiful always-out piece), three wood types (in addition to the maple, we tried walnut and cherry), and you can opt for features like juice and finger grooves. The feet are also optional, though they’re included by default, so you have to check a box if you want a board without feet.

What we’d leave: Again, this board is heavy, which makes it sturdy, but also a bit of a chore to clean. Because it’s wood, it also requires some upkeep in the form of oiling and buttering (the brand’s Board Butter has kept the surface of the Noah’s board in tip-top shape through months of use). Finally, while the feet are a vital feature, they do make the board a little less attractive if left on the counter with the juice groove facing up. But using the groove is a less frequent use than regular slicing and chopping, so you’ll be more likely to leave it feet side down—or at least turn it back over after you’re done cutting and cleaning.

According to recent reports, in the long run: With long-term testing of a full year, the Boardsmith has stood up in a way that justifies its high price. It’s held on to minimal stains, and with a bit of oil and wax every three to four weeks, the board looks as beautiful as it did when it arrived.

R-Board Series Rectangular Wooden Maple Cutting Board, 18”x12”.

Boos boards, as they’re commonly called, are pretty much the gold standard for wood cutting boards, and this relatively affordable maple cutting board is a dream to cut on.

In a recent development, what we love: Though maple is a hard wood, the cutting surface is smooth and has the perfect amount of give. In our testing, it seemed to almost embrace the knife blade with each chop. The board didn’t retain any food odors and it was easy to hand-wash (never put a wood board in the dishwasher!). Even beet juice disappeared after a good cleaning.

Boos Blocks come in many different sizes, we’ve found that the 18x12" size is just right for most home kitchens. This board is from the brand’s R-Board series, and it’s substantial without being too major. There’s plenty of room to carve a roast chicken, but it’s small enough to slide into the cabinet where you keep your sheet pans (a half-sheet is 18x13") as long as you don’t have too much else in there. At 2.25" it’s the tallest (thickest) cutting board we tested, and it will add significant height to your cooking zone, which is something shorter home cooks should always keep in mind when choosing a chopping board.

What we’d leave: Though not necessarily a negative, this board is on the heavy side (10 lb.), and it does require frequent oiling to keep it in tip-top shape. Boos recommends their proprietary Mystery Oil and Board Cream, and if you buy directly from the brand, you can bundle the care products with the board.

What we love: Sonder’s board is beautiful, and like the Boardsmith, it features end-grain construction, which is easier on knives because they slide between the wood fibers, avoiding friction with the hard surface. End-grain boards also “self-heal,” which means that the fibers come back together after having been sliced—and I found that after rigorous use in a week of endless chopping tests, this board came out looking as beautiful as it had when it came out of the package. This board is made of American walnut and constructed in the US.

In a recent development, the Sonder board also has some clever design elements: It’s hard to find an end-grain board that features a juice groove at this price point (the Boardsmith below, for example, costs almost $100 more). Flip the board over, and on the other side, it features three carved-out compartments, so you can slide chopped food to the side as you prep, keeping ingredients contained, separated, and out of the way. Those compartments can also be used for a fun charcuterie board setup: Use them to hold sauces and condiments or as a landing place for olive pits. Both sides of the board feature grippy rubber feet, and I found that this board stayed steady and level on the countertop even during heavy-duty chopping.

Industry observers note that this board was less cumbersome to take to the sink and hand wash than many of the large end-grain boards we tried. It has ergonomic handles carved into the sides, which makes for easy transport despite its heft and size. And because it’s a dark-colored wood, it highlights less sign of staining than other wooden boards.

What we’d leave: There’s not much fault to find in Sonder’s board beyond the standard caveats that an end-grain cutting board requires maintenance in the form of regular oiling and must be hand-washed. The prep grooves are a nice feature, but they aren’t as useful if you’re used to using a bench scraper, since it can’t fit in them. At $179, the Sonder is a bit pricey, but the benefits of end-grain over a cheaper edge-grain board are worth the bump up. If you’re concerned about price primarily, you should opt for the plastic Oxo board recommended below. Because of the carved-in prep containers on one side of the board, you have limited chopping space (but you always have the option to use the other side, which offers a full surface).

In a recent development, what we love: Senior reviews editor, Olivia Tarantino, owns three types of cutting boards (wood, composite, and the MK Midi), and the Midi is the one she grabs for anything short of a full dinner. “It’s closer to midsize than small, which makes it more versatile than a mini board that’s only good for smashing garlic. I can dice a whole onion, slice a tomato, and even fit a mise en place of scallion, ginger, and garlic. Because it’s nonporous, it’s my pick over wood for wetter ingredients, since I can toss it in the dishwasher when I’m done,” she claims, noting that she owns the white color and there’s no staining after eight months. The one downside worth noting is that the surface is a bit harder, which can be tougher on knives.

Adding a smaller board like this to a kitchen that already has a large wood cutting board can help for small prep work like slicing fruit, vegetables, or ingredients like garlic without having to clean your major board in between.

What we’d leave: We wish that Material would add feet to the larger version of the board. If it’s all you’ve got, a small cutting board can be frustratingly limiting. Also, after years of working with Material’s cutting boards in their homes, our editors noted that they will show visible wear and tear in the form of slice marks and small stains. This is inevitable for any plastic (or similar) cutting board.

Good Grips Plastic Utility Cutting Board.

In a recent development, what we love: This plastic cutting board from Oxo is very popular in the BA Test Kitchen. It’s budget-friendly and dishwasher-safe and comes with a juice groove. At 14.75" x 10.4", it’s a good size for meal prep, the plastic cutting surface is nonporous, and silicone strips run the length of both short sides to help keep it in place on the counter when cutting. It’s also reversible with one side offering a channel to catch meat juices.

According to recent reports, what we'd leave: The Oxo isn’t very attractive, so you wouldn’t want to use it as a serving board. Also, the longevity of a plastic board like this is only a couple of years, and if you chop too rigorously, the board has been known to shed plastic particles. If you are concerned about plastic use in the kitchen, this isn’t your board.

Yoshihiro Hi-Soft High Performance Professional Grade Cutting Board.

Rubber cutting boards are seen more often in professional kitchens than home ones, but if you’re looking for something large and durable, and you don’t want to have to bust out your knife sharpener regularly, consider this Hi-Soft rubber board by Yoshihiro. It’s very knife-friendly, and cutting on it feels nice. It stays in place on the counter, and unlike another rubber board we tested, it doesn’t have a rubber tire odor.

What we love: There are a couple of reasons chefs like food-safe rubber cutting surfaces. For starters, because rubber has a little give, the cutting surface flexes ever so slightly to the knife edge versus wearing it down like a hard surface would. Both synthetic and natural rubber are also nonporous, so they’re easier to sanitize than wood boards and are often used by sushi chefs for that reason (conversely, wood cutting boards are actually health-code violations in some cities).

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: Though sanitizing the surface is easy, large rubber boards can be harder to wash because, in addition to being big, they are also heavier than, say, plastic, and the rubber material must be washed by hand. Rubber cutting boards can also hold on to stains more easily than plastic.

Industry observers note that in the long run: With its light color this board has shown a bit of staining and evidence of knife blades running across it. But all things considered, it’s cleaned up very well and proven an excellent companion to an always-out end-grain wood board.

Before getting the knives out, we researched chopping boards and narrowed down a selection that included a wide range of plastic, rubber, and various types of wood boards that ranged from about $10 to almost $300.

Sources indicate that to assess the boards’ durability and stability, testers chopped a pound of carrots, diced a large onion, and minced fresh ginger. Testers also cut steamed beets on each board so they could see how much (or how little) each board held on to stains. We chopped lots of garlic on the boards and watched out over the course of the days and weeks of testing for odor retention on the boards. Finally, we washed each board according to the directions and oiled the wood boards that called for it.

Here is an example of the kind of staining you can expect with a wood cutting board. A good scrub with some coarse salt and lemon juice will help take care of this.

These are the qualities we looked for in the best cutting boards.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend that home kitchens have one large cutting board, ideally around 20" x 15". Additionally, it’s useful to have some supplemental smaller plastic or wood cutting boards (in the 16" x 12" and 12" x 8" ranges) that are easier to transport to the sink for washing or that fit in the dishwasher. You’ll have your bases covered when you have a large board that can take on any large cooking prep task without risk of vegetables flying all over the kitchen, or upon which you can plop a giant piece of meat for carving—but also some small boards that can be used daily for lighter prep, eliminating the need for a daily full-scale clean of your large board.

During testing, I also looked out for board height; if your board is too tall, it adds too much height to the counter, making it awkward for shorter home cooks to get a good angle when cutting. A too big or too heavy board is also hard to clean and move.

We recommend rubber, wood, and plastic cutting boards. There’s a trade-off involved in selecting the right hardness level for a cutting board. A material that’s too hard will have you busting out your knife sharpener more often than you should, while a board that’s too soft will end up with cut marks so deep you may no longer have a smooth surface—and it will be harder to clean and sanitize. So you want a durable surface that will feel nice to cut on and have some give. For wood cutting boards, we prioritized boards made with American materials. That’s particularly important because wood sourced abroad is often less sustainably sourced, first because it needs to be shipped overseas, and second because the US has more rigorous forestry regulations than some other countries. For a pro-and-con comparison of the various cutting board materials, scroll farther down the page.

It has been revealed that if the board had a special feature, like grippers or a juice channel, we evaluated how functional the features actually were. We measured the amount of liquid the juice grooves held and used any prep compartments.

Chop-N-Slice Series Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board, 18" x 12".

If you have your heart set on a Boos Board but don’t have a lot of space or want to spend a lot of money, this reversible board from the John Boos Chop-N-Slice series is a high-quality board with a pretty low price tag. It’s made of durable maple wood and arrives oiled (it only barely held on to stains from steamed beets). It’s only 1.25" thick, which contributes to its low price. Though it’s not too big or heavy, it has handle grooves on both ends, which can be helpful if you’re carrying a loaded board. Right out of the box, we felt the board was a little rough, but with a touch of seasoning, it significantly improved.

Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board.

In a recent development, this end-grain cutting board was a joy to chop on thanks to its soft and responsive surface—it genuinely felt the best of any of the wood boards we tested. Chopping feels ergonomic and your knife feels protected. The board is also beautiful and would stand proudly in a permanent place on anyone’s kitchen counter. When it arrived, it felt dry and chalky, so it immediately needed to be oiled and treated, whereas the winning end-grain boards felt more ready to go out of the box. And unlike the Boardsmith and Sonder boards, it doesn’t have a juice groove.

Recent findings suggest that it also seemed slightly uneven or warped from the beginning: The board wobbled back and forth ever so slightly during rigorous chopping, making a slight clanking noise. This was almost imperceptible, and since we’ve used Boos boards over the years and loved their stability and durability, we think it’s likely the flaw of the particular board we tested. So we’d still absolutely recommend Boos end-grain boards.

Large End Grain Prep Station Acacia Wood Cutting Board.

Sources indicate that this inexpensive end-grain board comes highly recommended by other review sites, and at $72 at the time of writing, it’s an excellent value for an acacia wood board. Its dark color makes it resistant to showing stains, and after being put through its chopping paces, it had no scratches. However, the board did arrive with a visible scratched-up patch on its lower right corner. Even though it was an end-grain board, I didn’t find it as soft or responsive as the Boos above or either of our winning boards. And the wood isn’t sourced domestically. Still, this is a solid value option.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a large and inexpensive board, this 20" x 15" option from TeakHaus is a good choice. The high-quality edge-grain teak looks great, and the darker wood won’t show stains like lighter-colored wood boards do. Cutting felt comfortable, and one side of this reversible board features a juice groove. It’s an inch-and-a-half tall, and that combined with the size makes it pretty bulky. Also, the smell of ginger lingered on this one a bit after we hand-washed it.

This Kickstarter-funded design isn’t just a cutting board; it’s a whole modular prep station. The cutting board has magnetic sides, onto which snap carved wood prep bowls fitted with stainless-steel containers (or silicone liners, depending on which package you opt for). Those bowls also stack nicely on top of the board for storage, and everything can be arranged and rearranged at the cook’s convenience.

According to recent reports, the design here is clever: It’s satisfying to move the board and containers around because everything fits together in a delightful little puzzle, and attaching the prep bowls produces a satisfying click. The magnetic connection is very secure, and it’s helpful and convenient to have little prep bowls available for sweeping away items as you chop them.

You can select various attachable container sizes, and there’s even a large one that runs the whole length of the cutting board that can be used to set up a dredging station for chicken cutlets. You can also buy lids that fit the containers so that they can go right in the fridge to store leftover prepped items, or sauces you made ahead of time for a dinner party.

In a recent development, we like a lot of what’s going on here, but the board’s edge-grain maple construction doesn’t feel high-quality—it was chalky and rough upon arrival. The system is available in a variety of wood types, so maybe the walnut or Brazilian teak that we didn’t test would fare better. But the system is pricey ($519 for a 13-piece set), and the space you’re offered on the actual cutting surface is limited, so there’s not a ton of room for actual chopping—you dedicate a lot of the counter real estate to the attachable containers. If you’ve been in the market for nice prep containers just as much as you have been for a cutting board and love the idea of a smartly designed holistic system, you’ll like the Chef Station. We love the design in theory, but on the merits of the cutting board alone, it’s not a test winner.

Maple Wood Kitchen Basic Cutting Board.

Industry observers note that the JK Adams Maple Wood Basic Cutting Board is made of durable maple. It has a minimal design with no embellishments and won’t add too much height to your prep zone. At just ¾" thick, it’s the thinnest wood board tested. The 17" x 14" footprint also offers a decent amount of space for cutting and chopping but is compact enough to keep in a small kitchen.

The JK Adams Pour Spout Cutting Board stands out because it has a juice groove and a pouring spout on both sides, making it truly reversible for cutting meat. Though this is a sizable board at 20" x 14", the groove and spout do take up a significant portion of the surface area available for cutting, so keep that in mind if you’re looking for something to use for really large cuts of meat. The wood is light-colored and will show stains from something like beets, but keeping it treated with beeswax and mineral oil will provide some stain resistance.

Material Kitchen’s MK Free Board is made entirely of plant-based materials ("100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers," according to Material’s website). That last part is notable—especially if you're concerned about microplastics—because this board has none, hence the name. It's dishwasher-safe and has a loop that makes it easy to pull out of a cabinet or hang from a hook. Overall, it’s a totally fine cutting board you can feel very good about using, but without some plant-based bumpers on the bottom, it won’t get a top spot in our rankings. While the microplastic-free material is wonderful in theory, it feels a bit harder on your knives, and because it doesn't have silicone corners, it’s more prone to sliding around on a quartz countertop. And without anything to soften its landing, the thinner, harder material is also fairly loud.

Silicone Cutting Boards Mats, Set of 3.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a nonporous alternative to plastic, rubber is our first pick. But both natural and synthetic rubber cutting boards are pricey, so you might want to consider a silicone cutting board. It’s notable to note that these are mats, not actual boards. But even at ⅛" thick, the material provided a reasonable barrier between the knife and counter. Silicone is flexible so it’s easy to fold into a U-shape to transfer ingredients to a pot or scraps to the trash. These mats are also dishwasher-safe even though they’re very easy to hand-wash. And since the entire mat is silicone, it’s very nonslip. These also have built-in grooves around the entire perimeter and a hole in the corner for hanging and so far, they haven’t held on to any stains (even from steamed beets) or shown any knife marks (even when we tried to make some). That noted, some customers on Amazon have reported knife damage to their mats, which could be a result of the silicone degrading. Though silicone is durable and heat tolerant, repeated exposure to high heat or sudden temperature changes can weaken its structural integrity, and it can hold on to stains.

The All Aboard cutting board from colorful cookware brand Great Jones is like the original Material reBoard’s bigger, curvier cousin. At 16" x 12", it’s significant for a plastic board, and it has a nice loop/handle for hanging. It’s made of BPA-free recycled plastic, and the textured surface is nice to cut on. It doesn't have any sort of silicone grip to keep it in place on the counter when cutting, but it does have a juice groove.

In a recent development, these double-sided boards come in three sizes; one side has a juice groove and the other has an indentation along the top intended to hold Caraway’s tiny Dot & Dash containers. The boards are made from eco-friendly birch, which is lightweight compared to other woods but feels more like maple when cutting. These boards are also pretty thin, so I have concerns about warping, though limiting exposure to moisture can help with that. The board also comes oiled, though it did hold on to some strawberry and beet stains—as we’d expect any wood board to do.

Architec Original Gripper Cutting Board.

According to recent reports, this 14" x 11" polypropylene (plastic) cutting board is fine but nothing special. It comes in a variety of fun colors, it has a handle hole you can use to hang it, and it’s dishwasher-safe. One side has small rubber feet (a.k.a. the “nonslip gripper” base), which does keep the board stationary but also makes it so you can only use one side for chopping.

Epicurean Kitchen Series Cutting Board.

As much as we love Epicurean’s multipurpose cooking utensil, the brand’s cutting board is a no-go. There’s much to like; the nonporous wood composite is dishwasher-safe and won’t warp or splinter like wood. Plus, it looks so much nicer than plastic. But one reason it’s so durable is that it’s so hard, which made everyone who tried it worry about their knife blades. It was also very loud to use. The pricier nonslip version (which also has a juice groove) was slightly more pleasant to use, but still not recommended.

But the light-colored wood stained fairly easily in testing and required intense scrubbing after we cut beets on it. And we no longer recommend bamboo cutting boards because the surface is extremely hard on knife edges.

Embedded between the two is a steel core to prevent the board from warping. Unfortunately, the board we received had hairline cracks which, without the steel core, would have probably knocked three corners off of this board. For such a pricey piece of gear, it wasn’t well-packaged for cross-country transit. But the fact that the board stayed fully intact even with three cracked corners is a testament to the strength of the steel core.

According to recent reports, made In’s tableware, cookware, and kitchen tools have a lot of fans at BA, and I wanted to love Made In’s edge-grain Butcher Block. One side is a solid butcher block surface without any grooves or embellishments, while the other features a juice groove. Industry observers note that the Totally Bamboo Kauai bamboo board is totally fine. It looks nice enough, it’s lightweight, and it doesn’t stain as easily as other wood cutting boards. But the surface is harder than comparable boards, and in testing, it slid around quite a bit on the counter. The Angled Board from Material, which is generally available in FSC-certified walnut or carbon wood (the latter is actually stained white oak), would certainly make an attractive addition to a modern kitchen. But in testing we found that the smooth laminate coating reveals knife marks quite easily. It was also surprisingly slippery when we were cutting vegetables.

Farberware Nonslip Plastic Cutting Board.

Despite its name, the Farberware Nonslip Cutting Board didn’t stay put on the countertop during testing. On the other hand, though it’s not entirely stable, it is a nice size (14" x 10"), and the plastic construction makes it dishwasher-safe.

Nicole Home Flexible Plastic Cutting Board Mats.

In a recent development, cutting boards (especially plastic ones) have one job, and that is to provide a protective layer between your knife and your counter. These flimsy “cutting board mats” didn’t, well, cut it in that department. They also slid around a lot when we were testing. If pressed, I’d say this type of cutting board (er, mat) could be handy to have around to put on top of a wood cutting board or butcher block countertop to help keep the wood clean and avoid cross-contamination when handling raw meat, but wouldn’t use this for chopping, slicing, or dicing directly on a stone countertop.

The first thing you need to decide on when choosing a cutting board is which material you prefer. Here’s a rundown of what's good and bad about each.

Sources indicate that PROS: Plastic cutting boards are useful as a supplement to a larger wooden board because they are lightweight and easy to carry around the kitchen. They are inexpensive, and they can go in the dishwasher. According to food director Chris Morocco, plastic is also a less absorbent material than wood (and about the same as rubber), which means they won’t harbor bacteria as easily. They’re a great choice for cutting raw meat.

CONS: Plastic boards are harder on your knives than wooden or rubber boards. They will also get dinged up after heavy use, which makes them prone to trapping bacteria. Plastic boards will need to be replaced more often than their wooden counterparts. Some research shows that microplastics in food could be linked to plastic cutting board use, but the research on the long-term health effects of microplastics remains unclear. You do run the risk of your cutting surface moving around a bit unless you go with one that’s designed to stay put like our top pick here. Chris recommends laying a damp dish towel, paper towel, or nonslip rubber mat under your plastic board to keep it steady. Again, we recommend using your plastic cutting boards supplementally, for less rigorous chopping tasks than your wooden chopping blocks.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: If you’re the kind of home cook who is a dishwasher devotee, isn’t quite ready to invest in a cutting board, or wants to cut up raw chicken one day and mince garlic the next and needs a board that can be a totally clean slate each time, then plastic boards are the pick for you.

PROS: In general, wood is soft enough to protect your chef’s knife but still hard enough for smooth cuts, making it perfect for prepping everything except raw meat, Chris states. (Though you can do that, too, if you’re willing to give them a thorough soapy hand-washing afterward.) Another thing we love about wood boards is that they tend to “heal” themselves (i.e., they close up those knife marks after use), which prevents germ-harboring grooves from forming and keeps them in good shape for longer.

CONS: These boards require the most maintenance because wood is the most absorbent board material out there. They’re prone to retaining odors and stains, which means cleaning and caring for them is extra notable—and requires more work than plastic or rubber. Scroll to the end for more on how to perform that care. We'll also note that an exception to the “easy on knives” rule is teak, which is a dense hardwood containing silica, a substance known to dull blades. So make sure to check which wood your board is made of, especially because teak boards tend to be less expensive.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Wood boards are best for those who care about beautiful objects and are game to give their kitchenware the care and attention it deserves—you know, the people who are regularly sharpening their knives, maintaining the seasoning on their cast-iron pans, and deep-cleaning their Dutch ovens.

According to recent reports, end-grain wood vs. Edge-grain wood.

It has been revealed that wood cutting boards come in two styles: edge-grain and end-grain. In edge-grain cutting boards, the wood grains are aligned horizontally. In end-grain boards, the wood fibers are aligned vertically. End-grain boards are easier on your knives, because the knife blade slips between the fibers of the board rather than sliding across them. End-grain boards also self-heal better than edge-grain boards, because the fibers can come back together. End-grain boards dry more swiftly than edge-grain boards because the individual fibers are more exposed to air. This means they require more regular oiling. However, they are also far less likely to crack than edge-grain boards.

According to recent reports, in previous versions of this review, we recommended edge-grain cutting boards because they tend to be less expensive. However, in our most recent enhancement we found plenty of end-grain boards that were within $20 to $30 dollars of their edge-grain competitors. Because the research really highlights that end-grain boards offer better longevity and are better for knife care, we’ve opted to recommend boards only in that style for our top picks this time around. Even if you invest in one that’s expensive (our favorite from Boardsmith), it will last you a very, very with proper care—the cost per use just makes sense.

Rubber cutting boards used to be found only in restaurant supply stores, but they have become more available on the market for regular home cooks in recent years—though they are still as expensive as wood boards.

Sources indicate that PROS: The rubber boards were some of our favorites in testing, because the material is so responsive. It’s lovely to slice on this springy surface. Rubber is soft, so it’s extremely easy on knives. The material is also non-porous, and therefore won’t absorb bacteria easily and is scratch resistant. They tend to have slightly textured surfaces, which is helpful for keeping them steady on the countertop. They’re super durable. While they aren’t usually dishwasher-safe, they don’t need any mineral oil applied (unlike wood cutting boards, which do); just wash them with mild detergent and leave them to air-dry.

It has been revealed that CONS: The only real cons here are that rubber cutting boards don’t have the luxe look and feel you get from a wood board. They also tend to be heavier and pricier than plastic ones.

In a recent development, there’s a reason these boards are so commonly found in sushi restaurants—the bouncy, softer surface supports a slicing motion rather than a rocking motion, making it optimal for ultra thin-bladed Japanese knives. If you like a heavier Western-style knife and use a rocking motion while chopping, this might not be the right board surface for you. Rubber boards are also quite heavy and difficult to maneuver around the kitchen, and they don’t look as nice as wooden boards.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Rubber cutting boards are great for people who like to use Japanese knives and want to invest in a piece of equipment that will last them for years to come, but doesn’t require a whole lot of upkeep.

Cutting board materials we don’t recommend.

How do you clean a plastic cutting board?

Industry observers note that as mentioned above, plastic cutting boards are the most low-maintenance option, as you can simply pop (most of) them in the dishwasher. Though, if you’re cutting meat or fish, you need to scrape off any remnants under cold water before throwing it in. In restaurant kitchens, people often have a metal scraper that looks a bit like a palette knife for this; your stainless-steel bench scraper or plastic pastry scraper can also work. It prevents the proteins from cooking into the board’s nooks and crannies in hot water.

How do you clean a rubber cutting board?

Use that same cold water scraping technique if you have a rubber board, then follow with a hot, sudsy soap-up. Both rubber and plastic boards can be left to air-dry because they aren’t prone to warping.

How do you clean a wood cutting board?

Wood cutting boards are a different story than any of the above materials. They’re high-maintenance–but also beautiful, long-lasting, and soft on your chef’s knife. Since you’re using your plastic or rubber board for raw meat (right?), a scrape-down followed by a warm, soapy hand-wash is usually enough for wood boards. Just don’t forget the underside. If you constantly get only one side of the board wet, you are unevenly hydrating the wood. Keep that same idea in mind when cutting: If your board is reversible, try to use both sides of it. If not, chop in different zones of your board to keep the surface evenly worn. That might sound like a lot, but if you chop in the same 2" quadrant daily, the angle on your board will promptly change, which can cause slippage and, eventually, dull knives. Drying is the last, crucial step. With a clean dish towel, dry your board as thoroughly as possible. Then prop it up on its side until bone-dry to further guard against warping or cracking.

Industry observers note that because knife-friendly wood can harbor bacteria and is prone to staining, an occasional sanitizing session is necessary—and if you are using your wood board for meat, those sessions should be more frequent. Sprinkle any stained areas with coarse salt and rub them with the cut side of half a lemon. To disinfect, dilute some white vinegar with water and spray the surface of your board. Let it sit for a couple minutes before washing and drying. If necessary, you can also sanitize your wood board with a bleach solution, but be sure to dry and then oil it really well after.

In a recent development, POST-CLEANING CARE: Beyond washing, wood boards need to be treated with some TLC. Step right this way for an in-depth explainer on how to clean and care for it, but here’s the gist: At least once a month, pull out a clean microfiber cloth, a food-grade mineral oil, and a food-safe board sealant that combines oil with a protective beeswax. This is just as true if you have an inexpensive teak, acacia wood as it is if you go with something pricier, like a cherry or walnut cutting board.

Industry observers note that rub a small bit of the oil onto every surface of your dry, clean board. (You want the board to be really dry before you do this, so as to not seal in moisture.) Follow with the balm, which will buff into a creamy consistency. Don’t wipe that away just yet. Leave your board to deep-condition overnight, and then in the morning, gently wipe away any extra with a cloth or paper towel.

Microfiber Cleaning Cloths, Pack of 12.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The American West may play host to the lion’s share of iconic national parks—Yosemite, Yellowstone, Grand Canyon—but Acadia National Park is the crown jewel of the East Coast. Despite being one of the most compact national parks in the country, it’s also one of the most frequented, with around four million visitors a year who journey here to experience its historic carriage roads and the rugged Atlantic coast.

Sources indicate that if you’re searching for a place to stay in proximity to the region’s dense forests and craggy coastlines, start by looking at the best Airbnbs near Acadia National Park. Offering more flexibility than a hotel—plus the possibility for true off-the-grid stays—the best homes are surrounded by nature. Winter travelers will want to bookmark amenities like fire pits and freestanding soaking tubs that make for a particularly cozy trip.

Because after all, while the park’s spring wildflower bloom and fall foliage peaks are spectacular—as are summer’s lush landscapes—winter offers a more reflective perspective ideal for recalibrating before (or after) a busy holiday season. Rather than competing with crowds for views, during the frosty months ahead, visitors can admire frozen ponds and snow-covered cliffs without another tourist in sight. And after a day of exploring, something about driving back to a snug cottage rental to relax beside a crackling fireplace feels especially luxurious.

For travelers searching for a scenic domestic escape this season, continue ahead for 11 atmospheric properties situated within driving distance of Acadia’s legendary trails.

The five-bedroom residence is especially well-suited for multigenerational families, thanks to a custom-built bunk bed room and open-concept game space.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, central heating, beach access, outdoor dining area, BBQ.

Homey amenities like a large picture window, freestanding bathtub, and crackling wood stove offer even more excuses to cozy up when you’re not outside exploring.

Take a snooze in the hammock, enjoy a refreshing outdoor shower, or hike right off the driveway into the national park—opportunities for enjoying nature here feel boundless.

Sources indicate that after a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

Expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

It has been revealed that to get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

Sources indicate that as your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”.

Inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

In a recent development, cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Industry observers note that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#134657. Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish ↗ Open Full Page

Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson.
  • From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.
  • In a recent development, cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

In a recent development, cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

Recent findings suggest that so, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s vital to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she stated. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

Lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

In a recent development, instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

Recent findings suggest that we’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson indicates not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

Industry observers note that “I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that between heading home for the holidays and booking a cold-weather getaway, we’re entering a busy season of travel. Recent news events notwithstanding, there’s always some stressor that accompanies flying, whether it’s too-crammed overhead bins or airline delays. Your suitcase, however, shouldn’t be on the list—and if yours has seen better days, give yourself one less thing to worry about by upgrading to a luggage set that can handle the trip.

While the right luggage won’t shorten the security line, it can make everything around it feel a lot easier (and, at the very least, look a lot better). Choose wisely, and you’ll have a streamlined duo that clears airline size requirements and is durable enough to handle any wear and tear from baggage handlers. Plus, with the holidays in mind, a suitcase set is also a great investment gift for the frequent flyer in your life; it’s just down to choosing the right one.

Ahead, eight luggage sets backed by Vogue editors to take you from the holidays to spring break and beyond.

Dimensions: 21.7”x 15.8”x 9.1” Colors available: 4 Materials: Anodized aluminum, hard-wearing plastic, polyester, and mesh.

Industry observers note that though Rimowa has been making luggage in Cologne, Germany, since 1898, its grooved aluminum case may be the most recognizable out of all the sets. The brand’s signature ridges first appeared in 1950, and the design has barely changed since.

Partially due to the iconic design, partially due to its spacious storage, it has also become the fashion set’s go-to baggage for traveling. While Rimowa doesn’t officially offer sets, you can pair the Original Cabin, which fits most overhead bins, with the Original Check-In, which is big enough for two weeks away, for $3,425 total. And with a lifetime guarantee, you’ll be passing these luggage pieces down for years.

A Vogue editor says: “My first significant-girl purchase was a three-piece Rimowa luggage set in green. At the time, I was traveling almost weekly and needed a reliable set that would take me away for up to three weeks at a time. More times than I can count, this set has come in handy through my travels; recently, I’ve been eyeing the trunk size to add to my collection.” —Minty Mellon, shopping market editor.

(If the brand’s carry-on looks familiar, it’s because they’ve made appearances on both Succession and The White Lotus.) The Luggage Set Hybrid pairs the Carry-on with the Check-in, at $1,425 for the two, both trimmed in Italian-made leather. Each case has a polycarbonate shell set into an aluminum frame, and the Japanese Hinomoto wheels roll silky across the terminal floor. The effect is minimal, quiet, and built to last.

A Vogue editor notes: “Carl Friedrik’s carry-on is the lightest, most stylish cabin bag I’ve ever owned. The wheels glide smoothly and the handle never sticks—a surprising rarity—and the exterior is thus far dent-free. I’m working my way up to the full set.” —Elly Leavitt, lifestyle shopping editor.

Recent findings suggest that paravel is officially back—and its Voyager Plus Travel Set is the closest you’ll get to stocking up for a trip in one fell swoop. Founders Indré Rockefeller and Andy Krantz, who met working at the Spanish fashion brand Delpozo, built the line around the Upcoming England coast, and the palette reflects that in simple shades of cream, navy, and Nantucket red. The shell is sturdy, made with recycled materials and aluminum-reinforced corners; plus a 10-year warranty, just in case. The Centenary line is the one to buy: Pair the Centenary Carry-On with the Centenary Medium Check-In, and you’ll have a set that looks like you found it at a Paris antique market.
